query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Mo content to x = 1 in the CoCrFeNiMox-Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3 composite will reduce both the friction coefficient and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range via enhanced solid-solution and second-phase strengthening and by promoting the formation of a continuous, high-temperature oxide/molybdate glaze.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniformly ball-milled powder mixtures containing 67.5 wt.% CoCrFeNiMox high-entropy-alloy matrix powder (x = 0.2, 0.5, or 1), 12.5 wt.% Ni-coated MoS2, 15 wt.% Ag, and 5 wt.% Cr2O3, mixed at 150 r/min for 8 h before sintering.
generation.intervention: Varying the Mo content, specifically increasing it to x = 1 (Mo1), during the SPS fabrication of the composite.
generation.conditions: Spark plasma sintering under vacuum and 40 MPa by heating to 1250 °C at 150 °C/min, holding for 3 min with furnace cooling; tribological tests conducted in air at temperatures from room temperature up to 800 °C (using an 8 N load, 4 mm rotation radius, 0.15 m/s sliding speed, and 270 m sliding distance against a 6 mm Si3N4 ball).
generation.structural_mediator: Increased Mo leads to Mo-induced FCC lattice distortion and promotes the formation of a hard, Mo-rich tetragonal σ phase. At high temperatures, oxidation and tribochemical reactions form a continuous glaze containing layered silver molybdates and other oxides.
generation.mechanism: Dissolved Mo impedes dislocation motion via solid-solution strengthening, and the formation of the rigid σ phase suppresses plastic deformation and scratching through second-phase strengthening. At lower temperatures, Ni/MoS2 provides a low-shear lubricating film and Ag reduces adhesion, while at high temperatures the formation of an oxide/molybdate glaze separates the contacting surfaces to lower interfacial shear and reduce material removal.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline Mo0.2 composite, the Mo1 composite is predicted to exhibit increased hardness and enhanced wear resistance due to the combined effects of lattice distortion and σ-phase formation, and the high-temperature formation of a dense oxide/molybdate glaze will further reduce the friction coefficient and wear rate, particularly at elevated temperatures (600–800 °C).
generation.baseline: The Mo0.2 composite, predominantly an FCC solid solution with minimal σ phase, which shows a friction coefficient of 0.66 at room temperature (peaking at 0.75 at 200 °C and dropping to 0.21 at 800 °C) and wear rates of 13.1 × 10^-6 mm³/N·m (room temperature), 98.1 × 10^-6 mm³/N·m (400 °C), and 6.6 × 10^-6 mm³/N·m (800 °C).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under dry sliding conditions in air with a Si3N4 counterface, using the specified SPS and tribological test parameters across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C. Note that while the Mo1 composite is expected to provide the best strength/wear balance overall, the friction reduction effect may vary, particularly in the 200–400 °C range.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the uniformity of friction reduction across the entire temperature range—particularly at intermediate temperatures (200–400 °C) where thermal softening and wear track effects might hinder lubricant layer formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate composites with Mo content x = 0.2 and x = 1 using the specified ball-milling and SPS conditions. Perform XRD to detect lattice distortion and σ-phase formation, SEM/EDS for phase distribution and wear-track mapping, Vickers hardness tests and compression tests, and conduct tribological ball-on-disk sliding tests over the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C. Raman spectroscopy should be used to identify the presence and continuity of the oxide/molybdate glaze, especially after high-temperature testing.
measurements: XRD peak shifts and detection of σ-phase peaks
SEM/EDS mapping of phases and wear tracks
Vickers hardness and compression stress–strain measurements
Profilometry for wear-scar dimensions and wear rate
Raman spectroscopy for identification of the glaze at 800 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, compared to the Mo0.2 baseline, the Mo1 composite does not exhibit increased hardness, formation of a well-defined σ phase, and if the friction coefficient and wear rate do not both show statistically significant decreases (particularly evident through the formation of a continuous glaze at high temperatures), then the hypothesis is rejected.
